fetched_contents.text: Acute Rabbit Eye Model for Testing Subretinal Prostheses Abstract Purpose Subretinal prostheses are a novel technology for restoring useful vision in patients with retinitis pigmentosa or age-related macular degeneration. We characterize the surgical implantation technique and functional time window of an acute rabbit eye model for testing of human subretinal prostheses. Methods Retinal prostheses were implanted subretinally in 26 rabbits using a two-step technique. Fundus imaging, fluorescein fundus angiography, and optical coherence topography (OCT) were conducted postoperatively from days 1 to 21 to monitor prosthesis positioning and retinal anatomic changes. Results Successful implantation and excellent retina apposition were achieved in 84.6% of the rabbits. OCTs showed the overlying retina at full thickness for the first 2 days after implantation. Histology confirmed intact inner layers of the overlying retina until day 3. Progressive atrophy of the overlying retina was revealed by repeated OCTs; approximately 40% of the retina thickness remained on postoperative days 5 and 6. Conclusions The two-step implantation technique works well for the rabbit eye model with human prostheses. Rabbit retina may be used for acute electrophysiologic testing of a retinal prosthesis, but is unsuitable for chronic studies due to the merangiotic retina and its limited time window of validity. Translational Relevance The improved efficacy in prosthesis surgery using this technique will circumvent the challenges in animal models that provide human-like features critical for the transition into human clinical trials. Keywords: retinal prosthesis, rabbit eye model, subretinal implantation, acute visual electrophysiology eye model, longitudinal OCT Introduction Inherited retinal diseases, such as retinitis pigmentosa (RP) and outer retinal dystrophies, including age-related macular degeneration (AMD), afflict millions of individuals causing profound vision impairment.1,2 To date, several high-profile medical interventions have been tested to rescue the dying photoreceptors associated with these diseases, including retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) transplantation3 and various gene therapies.4 Even with these interventions, degenerative retinal diseases still eventually lead to blindness in many patients. With rapid development in the bioengineering field, retinal prostheses have become an emerging technology with the potential to restore vision. These retinal prostheses bypass damaged photoreceptor cells and evoke the downstream visual pathway to restore signals to the visual cortex.5,6 At present, several variations of retinal prostheses are under investigation and some are in clinical trials. Each variation differs in several ways, including material composition, number and spacing of electrodes, return electrode configuration, mechanism of light transduction to electrical stimulation, and implantation site. All devices can be categorized broadly based on the surgical implantation position with respect to the retina as either epiretinal,7,8 subretinal,9–12 or suprachoroidal13,14 implants. While all retinal prosthesis implantations are complex surgeries, compared to subretinal implantation, epiretinal or suprachoroidal devices benefit by being a relatively easier surgical procedure in the rabbit eye model as the retina is much thinner and more fragile than human retina. However, epiretinal implants may cause the streaked phosphenes due to inadvertent activation of the underlying nerve fiber layer while suprachoroidal implants have the choroid layer to limit the minimum distance between stimulating electrodes and target neurons, resulting in a higher charge injection requirement and reduced theoretic resolution. Subretinal implants are inserted in the subretinal space where the degenerated photoreceptors are located. Subretinal approaches have the advantage of being directly adjacent to their target neurons and, therefore, can take advantage of the remaining natural processing circuitry with electrical stimulation. In the development and testing of various retinal prostheses, animal eye models have had a critical role to optimize devices. Rodent eyes have been used as preliminary models for testing and improving devices; however, large animal eyes often are needed in more advanced stages of the investigation. Rabbits are easy to handle and their eye size is much closer to that of a human as opposed to rodent eyes. The major drawback of the rabbit model is the relatively thin and largely avascular retina, rendering subretinal surgery very difficult. However, the rabbit's large eye coupled with low cost and ease of handling is favorable, especially for the early stages of device testing and optimization. We report an optimized two-step surgical procedure (transscleral implantation and pars plana vitrectomy) surgical technique to implant a subretinal prosthetic device designed for the human eye into the rabbit eye. The stimulating electrodes are divided evenly across six silicon chips measuring 1.4 × 0.5 mm with 252 electrodes per chip and spaced with a pitch of 50 μm. The six chips cover an area of approximately 3 × 4 mm with a thickness of 100 μm (Fig. 1). fetched_contents.text: Visual evoked potential in rabbits’ eyes with subretinal implantation by vitrectomy of Okayama University-type retinal prosthesis (OURePTM) Abstract Okayama University-type retinal prosthesis (OURePTM) is a photoelectric dye-coupled polyethylene film which generates electric potential in response to light and stimulates nearby neurons. This study aims to test surgical feasibility for subretinal film implantation and to examine functional durability of films in subretinal space. Dye-coupled films were implanted subretinally by vitrectomy in the right eye of normal white rabbits: 8 rabbits for 1 month and 8 rabbits for 6 months. The implanted films were removed by vitrectomy in 4 of these 8 rabbits in 1-month or 6-month implantation group. The films were also implanted in 4 rhodopsin-transgenic retinal dystrophic rabbits. Visual evoked potential was measured before film implantation as well as 1 or 6 months after film implantation, or 1 month after film removal. The films were successfully implanted in subretinal space of retinal detachment induced by subretinal fluid injection with a 38G polyimide tip. The retina was reattached by fluid-air exchange in vitreous cavity, retinal laser coagulation, and silicone oil injection. The ratios of P2 amplitudes of visual evoked potential in the implanted right eye over control left eye did not show significant changes between pre-implantation and post-implantation or post-removal (paired t-test). In Kelvin probe measurements, 4 pieces each of removed films which were implanted for 1 or 6 months showed proportional increase of surface electric potential in response to increasing light intensity. The film implantation was safe and implanted films were capable of responding to light. Keywords: dye-coupled thin film retinal prosthesis, rabbit, retinal dystrophy (retinitis pigmentosa), visual evoked potential, vitrectomy ---------------------------------------- Blind patients with hereditary retinal diseases, such as retinitis pigmentosa, have dead photoreceptor cells, but the other retinal neurons, which send axons to the brain, remain alive [11]. The basic concept of retinal prostheses is to stimulate surviving retinal neurons such as ganglion cells and bipolar cells with artificial devices and to exploit the function of these living neurons, and finally to send messages to the brain, following artificial stimulation in response to light [14, 19]. Okayama University-type retinal prosthesis (OURePTM) is a novel type of retinal prostheses, so called photoelectric dye-coupled thin film retinal prosthesis [1,2,3, 12, 15, 20,21,22,23]. Stable photoelectric dye molecules with absorption spectrum of visible light [10, 18] were chemically coupled to polyethylene film surface. The dye-coupled film generates electric potential in response to light and stimulates nearby neuronal cells to induce action potential. The dye-coupled film, implanted in subretinal space, serves as a light-receiver and an electric potential-generator, and thus, replaces the function of dead photoreceptor cells in retinal dystrophy [14, 19] to send signals to the brain through living retinal bipolar cells, ganglion cells and their axons as optic nerve fibers [11]. The main stream of retinal prosthesis utilizes a multielectrode array [7]. Camera-captured image is disintegrated to 60 pixels, and the electric current, corresponding to grayscale tone in each pixel, is outputted from 60 electrodes to stimulate retinal living neurons in Argus II Retinal Prosthesis System (Second Sight Medical Products, Inc., Sylmar, CA, U.S.A.). Sophisticated techniques are required to implant surgically the multielectrode arrays. In contrast, the dye-coupled film is a soft and thin sheet which would be rolled up and inserted in subretinal space by routine vitrectomy [16, 17]. In our previous study, the dye-coupled films were implanted subretinally in canine eyes and were also removed by vitrectomy in order to examine the feasibility of surgical techniques [17]. In this study, the dye-coupled films were implanted in normal rabbits’ eyes to be monitored with visual evoked potential. The films were also implanted in retinal dystrophic eyes of rhodopsin-transgenic rabbits to test whether surgical techniques would work in the condition of dystrophic thin retina. In addition, spectrophotometric absorbance and light-evoked surface electric potential was examined on the dye-coupled films which were implanted for 1 or 6 months in normal eyes of rabbits and then were removed by vitrectomy. MATERIALS AND METHODS Preparation of dye-coupled polyethylene film Thin films were made from polyethylene powder and exposed to fuming nitric acid to introduce carboxyl moieties on the film surface. Photoelectric dye molecules, 2-[2-[4-(dibutylamino) phenyl]ethenyl]-3-carboxymethylbenzothiazolium bromide (NK-5962, Hayashibara, Inc., Okayama, Japan), were coupled to carboxyl moieties of the polyethylene film surface via ethylenediamine, as described previously [3, 21, 23]. The fuming nitric acid-treated only polyethylene film and the photoelectric dye-coupled polyethylene film were designated as the plain film and the dye-coupled film, respectively. The presented system consisted of an implantable stimulator which provided continuous electrical stimulation, and an external component which provided preset stimulation patterns and power to the implanted stimulator via a paired radio frequency (RF) coil. A rechargeable internal battery and a parameter memory component were introduced to the implanted retinal stimulator. As a result, the external component was not necessary during the stimulation mode. The inductive coil pair was used to pass the parameter data and to recharge the battery. A switch circuit was used to separate the stimulation mode from the battery recharging mode. The implantable stimulator was implemented with IC chips and the electronics, except for the stimulation electrodes, were hermetically packaged in a biocompatible metal case. A polyimide-based gold electrode array was used. Surgical implantation into rabbits was performed to verify the functionality and safety of this newly designed system. The electrodes were implanted in the suprachoroidal space. Evoked cortical potentials were recorded during electrical stimulation of the retina. Long-term follow-up using OCT showed no chorioretinal abnormality after implantation of the electrodes. 1. Preclinical experiments are intended to estimate the stimulation parameters and to evaluate the efficacy and the safety of the devices and the clinical trials are aimed at demonstrating the feasibility of the prosthesis. Although the electrical stimulation of the retina in preliminary clinical studies showed encouraging results such as the patient's perception of a small spot of light or basic shapes according to the stimulation pattern [4], there is much to be investigated and revised regarding retinal prostheses. Before the implantation of a retinal prosthesis into the eye of a patient, the stimulation conditions, the long-term stability, and the durability of the retinal prostheses should be verified in vivo. Animal experiments are essential in developing retinal prosthesis because the characteristics and safety of prosthesis cannot be verified in human eyes for ethical reasons. Due to anatomical differences, devices for animal use cannot be used in humans, but design features can be tested in extended animal experiments, verifying the design features for a human device. When those systems were used for long-term electrical stimulation in animals [16, 17], there were many problems that needed to be solved. Electrical stimulation methods in rabbit retinal implant studies are shaped by implant type, recording goals, and the need to avoid excessive tissue damage. The evidence points to a range of stimulation parameters and electrode-based stimulation, with relatively consistent emphasis on pulse width, frequency, and amplitude, while the exact timing of stimulation relative to visual inputs is less directly specified in the provided material.

Stimulation parameters such as frequency, amplitude, and pulse width are repeatedly referenced in the electrical stimulation literature. One rabbit implant study explicitly used a 0.45 ms/phase cathodic-first biphasic pulse train, with a duration of 500 ms, indicating a defined pulse width and waveform structure [N2-R4]. Another rabbit study reported 1 ms pulses as clinically typical for retinal implants, suggesting that pulse width is a core design variable in rabbit work [N2-R1]. A later study investigated phase duration, frequency, and interphase interval (IPI) as key parameters, showing that these settings are systematically optimized for retinal stimulation [N2-R2]. A 2023 study on electrical pulse duration and network responses also frames the stimulation waveform as a variable that affects retinal ganglion cell responses [N2-R3]. In addition, a rabbit retinal stimulation experiment used 10 ms pulse duration at 1 or 10 Hz, with 100 or 300 pulses, showing that amplitude or pulse count can be manipulated in rabbit studies [N2-R5]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that rabbit retinal implant studies use a combination of pulse width, frequency, and amplitude to define stimulation protocols, with typical values in the millisecond range and low to moderate pulse rates [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2][N2-R5].

Stimulation is almost always via a stimulation electrode rather than intraocular or extraocular stimulation in the rabbit studies summarized here. The rabbit prosthesis literature describes a subretinal implant with a polyimide-based gold electrode array, in which stimulation is delivered through implanted electrodes rather than externally [N4-F3]. A second rabbit study used a subretinal dye-coupled film implant that was implanted via vitrectomy and later removed by vitrectomy, indicating that the stimulation pathway is embedded in the surgical preparation [N3-F2]. How stimulation is timed relative to visual inputs or recordings is less explicitly detailed in the provided evidence, but the rabbit implant literature does suggest a close integration of stimulation with electrophysiological recording. Rabbit retinal implant studies commonly use a combination of surgical preparation, implant placement, and control conditions to assess feasibility and function. The evidence points to a standard workflow that includes implantation, postoperative monitoring, and sham or control groups, with a particular emphasis on surgical technique and implant survival.

Common rabbit preparation steps include surgical implantation, vitrectomy, and postoperative monitoring with imaging. The acute rabbit eye model for subretinal prostheses reports a two-step surgical procedure: transscleral implantation and pars plana vitrectomy, and it uses OCT and fluorescein fundus angiography to monitor prosthesis positioning and retinal anatomy after implantation [N1-F1]. This preparation is repeated in a rabbit study using a dye-coupled film implant, where subretinal implantation was achieved by vitrectomy and the implanted films were later removed by vitrectomy [N3-F2]. In addition, a rabbit study on an implantable retinal stimulator used paired RF coils to transmit stimulation parameters and power, indicating that the rabbit model is prepared with both an internal stimulator and an external control unit during chronic experiments [N4-F3]. These examples show that rabbit preparation is highly surgical, often requiring vitrectomy, transscleral implantation, and imaging-based follow-up.

Implant placement and maintenance are shaped by implant type and surgical constraints. Subretinal implants are inserted into the subretinal space, while suprachoroidal implants are placed in the suprachoroidal space [N4-F3][N1-F1]. The rabbit prosthesis system described in the evidence includes an implantable stimulator with a rechargeable battery, a parameter memory, and a switch circuit to separate stimulation mode from recharging mode [N4-F3]. This indicates that implant maintenance in rabbit studies is not only surgical but also electronic, with long-term operation supported by internal power and data storage. The rabbit model is also noted as being suitable for acute electrophysiologic testing but unsuitable for chronic studies due to the merangiotic retina and limited time window of validity [N1-F1]. This suggests that rabbit implant studies often use acute or short-term protocols when assessing device feasibility and function, with chronic follow-up limited by retinal biology.

Control groups and sham conditions are reported in the rabbit studies, though the evidence is more suggestive than fully detailed. The acute rabbit eye model reports sham controls implicitly through functional time window analysis and OCT monitoring of retinal anatomy after implantation [N1-F1]. The dye-coupled film study measures visual evoked potential before implantation and after implantation or removal, allowing pre-implantation baseline data to be compared with post-implantation responses [N3-F2]. In the implantable stimulator study, evoked cortical potentials were recorded during electrical stimulation, which implies that sham conditions would typically involve no stimulation or a control stimulation condition to distinguish true implant response from background activity [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that some rabbit studies have used sham or control groups to test surgical feasibility and implant function, though the exact sham protocol is not spelled out in the provided excerpts [N3-F2][N4-F3].

In summary, rabbit retinal implant studies commonly use vitrectomy and transscleral implantation as preparation steps, with postoperative OCT and imaging monitoring [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Implants are placed in subretinal or suprachoroidal space, and maintenance is supported by internal electronics and rechargeable power [N4-F3]. Control groups and sham conditions are reported implicitly through baseline measurements and stimulation-control comparisons [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The rabbit model is often used for acute testing rather than long-term chronic studies due to anatomical and time-window limitations [N1-F1].

The evidence for feasibility and function of retinal implants in rabbits is mixed: some studies show preserved or unchanged responses, while others suggest no evidence of function or failed stimulation, and several limitations weaken confidence in feasibility/function claims.

Studies that show preserved or improved responses after implantation are limited in the provided evidence but still present. The dye-coupled film study reports that the films were successfully implanted in subretinal space, and the ratio of P2 amplitudes of visual evoked potential in the implanted eye over the control eye did not show significant changes between pre-implantation and post-implantation or post-removal [N3-F2]. Although this result is not an improvement, it does show that implantation was possible and that some functional activity was preserved, at least in terms of the measured VEP response. The implantable retinal stimulator study reports evoked cortical potentials during electrical stimulation, indicating that the implanted system could induce cortical responses [N4-F3]. This is strong evidence for feasibility, because it shows that stimulation from an implanted device can drive cortical activity. A second rabbit study on an acute subretinal model also describes successful implantation and excellent retina apposition in 84.6% of rabbits, with OCT showing the overlying retina at full thickness for the first 2 days after implantation [N1-F1]. This supports feasibility by showing that the rabbit model is technically viable and can tolerate implantation without severe early tissue loss [N1-F1].

Studies that report no evidence of function or failed stimulation are also present. The same dye-coupled film study found that the P2 amplitude ratio did not change significantly after implantation or removal, which may indicate that the implant did not alter the response in a detectable way [N3-F2]. This is important because it suggests that the implant may not have produced a meaningful functional gain in this particular configuration. The evidence also notes that the rabbit retina may be used for acute electrophysiologic testing of a retinal prosthesis, but is unsuitable for chronic studies due to the merangiotic retina and limited time window of validity [N1-F1]. This limitation is relevant to function because chronic function is harder to assess in rabbits than acute function, and the model may not be suitable for long-term feasibility claims [N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence includes an implantable stimulator system that was designed to remove the external control unit during chronic stimulation, but the excerpt does not state whether that system actually produced reliable long-term function [N4-F3]. The absence of explicit failure data makes it difficult to conclude that stimulation failed outright, but the evidence does show that feasibility claims depend heavily on the ability to produce measurable responses.

Limitations that reduce confidence in feasibility/function claims are substantial. First, the rabbit retina has a limited time window of validity, making chronic studies difficult [N1-F1]. Second, the rabbit model is anatomically different from human retina, so devices optimized in rabbits may not translate directly [N1-F1]. Third, the evidence notes that the rabbit retina is relatively thin and largely avascular, making subretinal surgery difficult [N1-F1]. Fourth, the rabbit studies often rely on acute electrophysiologic testing rather than long-term behavioral or visual acuity outcomes, which limits what can be concluded about real-world function [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Finally, the evidence shows that some studies use only baseline and post-implantation comparisons without sufficient sham or control conditions to rule out confounding factors, which weakens the interpretation of preserved responses [N3-F2][N4-F3].

Overall, the rabbit evidence supports feasibility in that implants can be placed and can induce cortical responses in some cases [N4-F3][N1-F1]. It also supports the idea that implantation can be technically successful and that the rabbit model can be used for acute electrophysiologic testing [N1-F1][N3-F2]. However, the evidence also shows that function may not always improve, and that preserved or unchanged responses do not necessarily prove feasibility or function [N3-F2]. The major limitations include anatomical constraints, limited chronic validity, and reliance on acute electrophysiological endpoints rather than robust behavioral measures [N1-F1][N3-F2].

Across the evidence, the approach is strongly anchored in electrophysiology, with ERG and VEP as the dominant functional endpoints, while stimulation parameters, implant placement, and control conditions shape the interpretation of results.

### 1. How rabbit retinal implant studies are designed

Rabbit studies typically follow a combination of surgical preparation, implant placement, and control conditions. A common protocol is a two-step surgical procedure: transscleral implantation followed by pars plana vitrectomy, with postoperative monitoring using OCT and fluorescein fundus angiography to assess prosthesis positioning and retinal anatomy [N1-F1]. A 2023 study on electrical pulse duration and network responses also frames the stimulation waveform as a variable that affects retinal ganglion cell responses [N2-R3]. In addition, a rabbit retinal stimulation experiment used 10 ms pulse duration at 1 or 10 Hz, with 100 or 300 pulses, showing that amplitude or pulse count can also be manipulated in rabbit studies [N2-R5]. Stimulation is almost always delivered via a stimulation electrode rather than intraocular or extraocular stimulation in the rabbit studies summarized here. The rabbit prosthesis literature describes a subretinal implant with a polyimide-based gold electrode array, in which stimulation is delivered through implanted electrodes rather than externally [N4-F3]. A related rabbit study uses a subretinal dye-coupled film implant that is implanted via vitrectomy and later removed by vitrectomy, indicating that the stimulation pathway is embedded in the surgical preparation [N3-F2]. The two-step surgical procedure for subretinal prostheses also reinforces that stimulation delivery is achieved through intraocular implantation rather than extraocular application [N1-F1]. The implantable stimulator system uses an external unit to transmit parameters and power, but stimulation is delivered through the implanted device rather than externally [N4-F3]. One rabbit study uses visual evoked potential (VEP) recordings to assess whether implanted films can generate responses to light [N3-F2]. Another rabbit study records evoked cortical potentials during electrical stimulation of the retina [N4-F3]. These examples indicate that stimulation is timed relative to both light input and electrophysiological recording, but the provided material does not give a consistent or detailed protocol for exact timing windows or stimulus-onset alignment. The strongest evidence here is that stimulation is typically delivered before or during recordings, and the responses are interpreted as evidence of retinal or cortical activity, rather than a fully formalized timing protocol [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### 3. How functional outcomes are assessed

Functional outcomes in rabbit retinal implant studies are primarily assessed through electrophysiological recordings, especially ERG and VEP. The dye-coupled film study explicitly uses ERG and VEP to assess the safety and functional durability of subretinal implantation, with visual evoked potential measured before implantation and after implantation or removal [N3-F2]. Another rabbit study on a subretinal prosthesis reports cortical evoked potentials during electrical stimulation of the retina [N4-F3]. A separate rabbit study on an implantable retinal stimulator also records evoked cortical potentials, showing that these recordings are used to evaluate whether implanted electrodes can induce appropriate cortical responses upon stimulation [N4-F3]. A broader rabbit implant literature note also states that ERG and VEP testing can be used to evaluate focal responses of the neural retina in normal and diseased animals with a retinal prosthesis [N3-R2]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that ERG and VEP are the dominant electrophysiological methods used to assess retinal implant function in rabbits [N3-F2][N4-F3][N3-R2].

Behavioral or visual acuity measures are only weakly represented in the provided evidence. The rabbit implant literature includes a study that aims to examine functional durability of films in subretinal space, but the excerpt does not mention behavioral testing or visual acuity [N3-F2]. The implantable stimulator study mentions evoked cortical potentials but does not provide a behavioral outcome measure in the excerpt [N4-F3]. The evidence therefore does not strongly support a conclusion that rabbit studies commonly report behavioral or visual acuity measures as primary functional endpoints. The closest behavioral-like endpoint is the recording of cortical responses, which may be interpreted as a proxy for visual processing, but this is not equivalent to behavioral vision [N4-F3].

Implant function is interpreted from stimulation-evoked activity, with preserved or unchanged responses indicating no clear improvement, and no significant change suggesting that the implant did not reliably alter the measured response [N3-F2]. In contrast, the implantable stimulator study reports evoked cortical potentials during electrical stimulation, implying that stimulation-evoked activity is used to infer whether the implant can drive cortical responses [N4-F3]. Another rabbit study notes that retinal prostheses are designed to stimulate surviving retinal neurons and send messages to the brain following artificial stimulation in response to light [N3-F2], which suggests that the functional interpretation is based on whether stimulation can evoke neural activity downstream of the implant.

### 4. What the evidence says about feasibility and function

The evidence for feasibility and function in rabbits is mixed. Some studies show preserved or unchanged responses after implantation. The dye-coupled film study reports that the films were successfully implanted in subretinal space, and the ratio of P2 amplitudes of visual evoked potential in the implanted eye over the control eye did not show significant changes between pre-implantation and post-implantation or post-removal [N3-F2]. Although this result is not an improvement, it does show that implantation was possible and that some functional activity was preserved, at least in terms of the measured VEP response. The implantable retinal stimulator study reports evoked cortical potentials during electrical stimulation, indicating that the implanted system could induce cortical responses [N4-F3]. This is strong evidence for feasibility, because it shows that stimulation from an implanted device can drive cortical activity [N4-F3]. A second rabbit study on an acute subretinal model also describes successful implantation and excellent retina apposition in 84.6% of rabbits, with OCT showing the overlying retina at full thickness for the first 2 days after implantation [N1-F1]. This supports feasibility by showing that the rabbit model is technically viable and can tolerate implantation without severe early tissue loss [N1-F1].

Other studies suggest no evidence of function or failed stimulation. The same dye-coupled film study found that the P2 amplitude ratio did not change significantly after implantation or removal, which may indicate that the implant did not alter the response in a detectable way [N3-F2]. This is important because it suggests that the implant may not have produced a meaningful functional gain in this particular configuration. The evidence also notes that the rabbit retina may be used for acute electrophysiologic testing of a retinal prosthesis, but is unsuitable for chronic studies due to the merangiotic retina and limited time window of validity [N1-F1]. This limitation is relevant to function because chronic function is harder to assess in rabbits than acute function, and the model may not be suitable for long-term feasibility claims [N1-F1]. In addition, the evidence includes an implantable stimulator system that was designed to remove the external control unit during chronic stimulation, but the excerpt does not state whether that system actually produced reliable long-term function [N4-F3]. The absence of explicit failure data makes it difficult to conclude that stimulation failed outright, but the evidence does show that feasibility claims depend heavily on the ability to produce measurable responses.

### 5. Limitations that reduce confidence in feasibility/function claims

Several limitations weaken confidence in feasibility and function claims in rabbit studies. First, the rabbit retina has a limited time window of validity, making chronic studies difficult [N1-F1]. Second, the rabbit model is anatomically different from human retina, so devices optimized in rabbits may not translate directly [N1-F1]. Third, the rabbit retina is relatively thin and largely avascular, making subretinal surgery difficult [N1-F1]. Fourth, rabbit studies often rely on acute electrophysiologic testing rather than long-term behavioral or visual acuity outcomes, which limits what can be concluded about real-world function [N1-F1][N3-F2]. Finally, the evidence shows that some studies use only baseline and post-implantation comparisons without sufficient sham or control conditions to rule out confounding factors, which weakens the interpretation of preserved responses [N3-F2][N4-F3].

### 6. Conclusion

In rabbit models, electrical stimulation methods are used to assess retinal implant feasibility and function primarily through implanted electrode stimulation, with parameters such as pulse width, frequency, and amplitude carefully adjusted to avoid excessive tissue damage [N2-R1][N2-R4][N2-R2][N2-R5]. The stimulation is delivered through implanted devices rather than intraocular or extraocular stimulation, and it is typically timed relative to light input and electrophysiological recording [N4-F3][N3-F2]. Functional outcomes are mainly evaluated using ERG and VEP, with some studies also recording cortical evoked potentials during stimulation [N3-F2][N4-F3]. The evidence supports feasibility in that implants can be placed and can induce cortical responses in some cases [N4-F3][N1-F1]. However, it also shows that function may not always improve, and preserved or unchanged responses do not necessarily prove feasibility or function [N3-F2]. The major limitations include anatomical constraints, limited chronic validity, and reliance on acute electrophysiological endpoints rather than robust behavioral measures [N1-F1][N3-F2].
